# How the Iran Conflict Is Disrupting Global Supply Chains

How the Iran Conflict Is Disrupting Global Supply Chains

The ongoing Iran conflict has the potential to significantly disrupt global supply chains. As the Middle East is a key hub for energy production and international shipping routes, instability in the region can have widespread economic consequences.

From rising energy prices to disrupted shipping routes, the Iran conflict could create major challenges for supply chain professionals, procurement teams and global businesses.

## Why the Strait of Hormuz Matters for Global Trade

One of the most critical factors is the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow shipping route between Iran and Oman. It is one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints, with around a quarter of global crude oil shipments passing through it daily.

If conflict restricts traffic through this route, global energy supply can be affected almost immediately. Military escalation in the region has already led to disruptions in oil and natural gas shipments, contributing to rising energy prices.

0-72h procurement disruption response

Sanctions-adjacent supplier payment hold creates supply disruption
Geopolitical shock increases sanctions risk. Treasury considers payment hold. Supplier threatens shipment hold. Legal requires ownership screening. Procurement has short inventory runway. Accounting may need disclosure if disruption crosses materiality.
Decision should be framed as payment/legal/supply trade-off, not isolated sanctions or treasury issue.

Critical supplier payment due within 10 days during bank disruption
Payment is due soon to a critical supplier. Beneficiary bank is in an affected country. Payment could be delayed by sanctions screening or bank closure; supplier may stop shipment if unpaid.
Escalate Treasury/Legal/Procurement joint review; do not issue single-mode payment recommendation.

Tier-1 supplier unaffected but sub-tier material concentrated
Tier-1 supplier reports no disruption, but underlying material is likely sourced from a region affected by export restrictions.
Sub-tier unknown should be treated as significant; generate hypotheses and ask procurement for BOM/sub-tier confirmation.

Single-source component disrupted by natural disaster
A critical component is sourced from one supplier in an affected region. Alternative source exists but is not approved and qualification takes months.
Supplier substitution friction is high; decision should focus on inventory runway, customer prioritization and qualification acceleration.

Cash trapped in affected subsidiary after capital control announcement
A subsidiary holds book cash in a jurisdiction where capital controls are announced. Group treasury wants to fund another region but transfer route and local permission are unknown.
Treat cash as uncertain availability until transfer route is confirmed; exclude from unrestricted liquidity in stress case.
